glance.label: Main Idea
glance.html: Jesus answers John’s question from prison by pointing to His works, honors John as the promised forerunner, exposes a generation that rejects both of them, pronounces woes on unrepentant cities, and invites the weary to come to Him for rest.

glance.label: Setting
glance.html: Matthew 11 begins the third movement, The King Meets Rejection and Recognition (11:2–16:20). John the Baptist is in Herod Antipas’s prison while Jesus continues to teach in Galilee’s cities.

glance.label: Chapter Outline
glance.html:
• Matthew 11:1 — Jesus Finishes Instructing the Twelve

  • Matthew 11:2–6 — John’s Question from Prison

  • Matthew 11:7–15 — Jesus Honors John the Baptist

  • Matthew 11:16–19 — This Generation Rejects Both John and Jesus

  • Matthew 11:20–24 — Woes on the Unrepentant Cities

  • Matthew 11:25–30 — The Son Reveals the Father and Gives Rest

glance.label: Key Verse
glance.html: “Come to Me, all you who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.” (Matthew 11:28)

cards.title: The Heart of the Chapter
cards.html:
Even John the Baptist has a question. From prison he sends to ask, “Are You the Coming One, or do we look for another?” (11:3). Jesus does not rebuke him. He points to what is happening: the blind see, the lame walk, the dead are raised, and the poor hear good news, just as Isaiah promised. Then He honors John publicly as more than a prophet, the messenger who prepared His way. Faithful servants can bring honest disappointment to Jesus, and He answers with His word and works.

Not everyone responds so well. This generation is like children who will neither dance nor mourn. John fasted and they called him demon-possessed. Jesus ate with sinners and they called Him a glutton. Chorazin, Bethsaida, and Capernaum saw His mighty works and still did not repent, and their accountability is greater than Sodom’s. Yet the chapter ends with the Son praising the Father for revealing these things to babes. No one knows the Father except the Son and those to whom He reveals Him, and the Son invites all who labor and are heavy laden to come and find rest under His gentle yoke.

cards.title: Chapter Sections
cards.html:
Matthew 11:1 — Jesus Finishes Instructing the Twelve

Having finished instructing the Twelve, Jesus moves on to teach and preach in their cities.

Matthew 11:2–6 — John’s Question from Prison

John, in prison, sends disciples to ask whether Jesus is the Coming One. Jesus answers with the works Isaiah foretold and blesses the one who does not stumble because of Him.

Matthew 11:7–15 — Jesus Honors John the Baptist

Jesus honors John as more than a prophet, the messenger of Malachi who comes in the role of Elijah. Yet the least in the kingdom of heaven has a greater privilege, and the kingdom has suffered violence since John’s ministry began.

Matthew 11:16–19 — This Generation Rejects Both John and Jesus

Jesus compares His generation to children who reject every game. They dismissed John’s austerity and Jesus’ table fellowship alike, but wisdom is justified by her children.

Matthew 11:20–24 — Woes on the Unrepentant Cities

Jesus pronounces woes on Chorazin, Bethsaida, and Capernaum, where most of His mighty works were done. Because they did not repent, their judgment will be heavier than that of Tyre, Sidon, and Sodom.

Matthew 11:25–30 — The Son Reveals the Father and Gives Rest

Jesus thanks the Father for revealing these things to babes and declares that only the Son knows and reveals the Father. He invites the weary to come to Him, take His yoke, learn from Him, and find rest for their souls.

cards.title: Why This Chapter Matters
cards.html:
Matthew 11 shows how Jesus treats a struggling servant. John’s circumstances did not match his expectations, and Jesus answered him with evidence, not condemnation. The chapter also warns that seeing great light without repenting brings greater accountability.

Above all, the chapter reveals the heart of the King. The One who alone knows the Father invites the weary and burdened to come. He gives rest from the burden of sin when people come to Him, and He teaches a deeper rest as they take His yoke and learn His meekness and lowliness. His rule is not opposed to rest. Pride, self-reliance, and the need to prove oneself are heavier burdens than His yoke.

cards.title: Key Themes to Watch For
cards.html:
Honest questions. John brings his doubt to Jesus and receives an answer from His works (11:2–6).

John’s place. The forerunner stands between the prophets and the kingdom’s arrival (11:9–14).

Rejection. This generation refuses both John and Jesus (11:16–19).

Accountability for light. The cities that saw His works face heavier judgment (11:20–24).

Revelation and rest. The Son reveals the Father and gives rest to the weary (11:25–30).

cards.title: Key Words & Concepts
cards.html:
The Coming One (11:3). A title for the expected Messiah. John wants to know whether Jesus is the One he announced.

Suffers violence (11:12). The best reading in this setting is violent opposition against the kingdom and its messengers, seen in John’s imprisonment. The wording also allows a reference to the kingdom’s forceful advance.

Elijah who is to come (11:14). Malachi 4:5 promised Elijah before the day of the LORD. John was not Elijah returned in person (John 1:21), but he came in Elijah’s spirit and power (Luke 1:17).

Woe (11:21). A cry of grief and warning that announces coming judgment.

Yoke (11:29). The wooden frame that joins an animal to its work. Jesus’ yoke is His rule and way of life, carried in relationship with Him.

focus: Matthew 11 marks the turn from Jesus’ instructions to the Twelve to a movement of rejection and recognition, as Jesus answers John the Baptist’s question from prison by pointing to His works, honors John as the promised messenger, and rebukes a generation and its cities for refusing to repent. The chapter ends as Jesus thanks the Father for revealing these things to babes and invites all who labor and are heavy laden to come to Him for rest.

sections.title: Jesus Finishes Instructing the Twelve
sections.summary: When Jesus finishes commanding His twelve disciples, He departs to teach and to preach in their cities. The verse closes the discourse of Matthew 10 and returns the narrative to Jesus’ own ministry.

sections.title: John’s Question from Prison
sections.summary: Hearing in prison about the works of Christ, John sends his disciples to ask, “Are You the Coming One, or do we look for another?” (Matthew 11:3). Jesus tells them to report what they hear and see, that the blind see, the lame walk, the dead are raised, and the poor have the gospel preached to them, and He adds, “And blessed is he who is not offended because of Me” (Matthew 11:6).

sections.title: Jesus Honors John the Baptist
sections.summary: Jesus asks the multitudes what they went out to the wilderness to see and declares that John is more than a prophet, the messenger of whom it is written who prepares His way. No one born of women is greater than John, yet he who is least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he, and if they are willing to receive it, John is the Elijah who is to come.

sections.title: This Generation Rejects Both John and Jesus
sections.summary: Jesus likens this generation to children in the marketplaces who complain that others will neither dance to the flute nor mourn to a lament. They say John has a demon because he came neither eating nor drinking, and they call the Son of Man a glutton, a winebibber, and a friend of tax collectors and sinners, but wisdom is justified by her children.

sections.title: Woes on the Unrepentant Cities
sections.summary: Jesus rebukes the cities where most of His mighty works were done because they did not repent. He declares that the judgment will be more tolerable for Tyre, Sidon, and Sodom than for Chorazin, Bethsaida, and Capernaum.

sections.title: The Son Reveals the Father and Gives Rest
sections.summary: Jesus thanks the Father for hiding these things from the wise and prudent and revealing them to babes, and He declares that no one knows the Father except the Son and the one to whom the Son wills to reveal Him. He then invites, “Come to Me, all you who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28), and He adds that those who take His yoke upon them and learn from Him, for He is gentle and lowly in heart, will find rest for their souls.

1.brief: When Jesus finishes instructing His twelve disciples, He leaves to teach and preach in their cities. The mission discourse closes, and Jesus Himself continues the work He has just sent His disciples to share.
1.explain:
“Now it came to pass, when Jesus finished commanding His twelve disciples,”

Jesus has finished instructing the Twelve. Matthew marks the end of each of Jesus’ five major teaching sections with similar words (7:28; 13:53; 19:1; 26:1).

“that He departed from there to teach and to preach in their cities.”

Jesus does not stop working while the disciples go out. He continues His own ministry of teaching and preaching in the towns of Galilee.
1.notes: The phrase in their cities likely refers to the towns of Galilee.

2.brief: While in prison, John hears about the works of Christ and sends two of his disciples to Him. The faithful forerunner, now suffering for his ministry, brings his question to Jesus Himself.
2.explain:
“And when John had heard in prison about the works of Christ,”

John the Baptist is “in prison.” Herod Antipas had arrested him for condemning Herod’s marriage to his brother’s wife (14:3–4). From prison, John hears about “the works of Christ,” the deeds Matthew has recorded in chapters 8–9.

“he sent two of his disciples”

John cannot come himself, so he sends two of his followers to Jesus.
2.notes:
The Jewish historian Josephus says that John was imprisoned at Machaerus, a fortress east of the Dead Sea.

Matthew calls Jesus Christ here, the Greek form of Messiah. He identifies Jesus as the One whose works John has heard about.

3.brief: Through his disciples John asks, “Are You the Coming One, or do we look for another?” Jesus answers by pointing to His works; John’s imprisonment may not have matched what he expected of the Messiah, though Matthew does not state his exact reasons for asking.
3.explain:
“and said to Him, ‘Are You the Coming One, or do we look for another?”

John’s question is direct. “The Coming One” was a title for the Messiah. John had announced One coming after him who would baptize with the Holy Spirit and fire and bring judgment (3:11–12).

Now John is in prison. Jesus is healing and preaching, but He has not overthrown the wicked or set John free. John may have wondered why Jesus did not look like the Messiah he expected. He brings his question honestly to Jesus.
3.notes: Psalm 118:26 says, “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD!” The crowds will shout these words at Jesus’ entry into Jerusalem (21:9).

4.brief: Jesus tells the messengers to go and report to John what they hear and see. He answers not with a bare claim but by pointing to the evidence of His works.
4.explain:
“Jesus answered and said to them, ‘Go and tell John the things which you hear and see:”

Jesus does not answer with a simple yes. He tells the messengers to report what they “hear and see.” His works will speak for themselves.
4.notes: Luke 7:21 adds that in that same hour Jesus cured many of infirmities and afflictions and gave sight to many who were blind.

5.brief: The blind see, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised, and the poor hear the gospel. These works echo Isaiah’s promises of the Messiah’s day, showing John that God’s promised salvation has arrived in Jesus.
5.explain:
“The blind see and the lame walk; the lepers are cleansed and the deaf hear;”

Jesus describes His works in words that echo Isaiah’s prophecies. Isaiah promised that in the day of God’s salvation the eyes of the blind would be opened, the ears of the deaf unstopped, and the lame would leap like a deer (Isaiah 35:5–6).

“the dead are raised up and the poor have the gospel preached to them.”

Jesus adds two more signs: life for the dead and good news for the poor. The second echoes Isaiah 61:1, where the Anointed One is sent to preach good news to the poor.

John knew these prophecies. Jesus is telling him that the promises are being fulfilled. The Messiah has come.
5.notes: Isaiah 35 also speaks of God coming with vengeance (Isaiah 35:4), and Isaiah 61:2 speaks of the day of vengeance. Jesus’ answer emphasizes salvation. The judgment John announced will come, but not yet.

6.brief: Jesus adds, “blessed is he who is not offended because of Me.” He gently encourages John and all who hear to trust Him even when His way does not meet their expectations.
6.explain:
“And blessed is he who is not offended because of Me.”

Jesus ends with a gentle word for John. “Offended” means caused to stumble. The person who does not stumble over Jesus, even when He does not meet every expectation, will be blessed.
6.notes: The Greek word translated “offended” gives us the English word scandal. It describes something that trips a person up.

7.brief: As the messengers leave, Jesus asks the crowds what they went into the wilderness to see, “A reed shaken by the wind?” John was no wavering man swayed by every pressure.
7.explain:
“As they departed, Jesus began to say to the multitudes concerning John:”

After John’s messengers leave, Jesus speaks to the crowd about John. He does not want them to think less of John because of his question.

“What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A reed shaken by the wind?”

Many had gone out to the wilderness to hear John. Jesus asks what they expected. “A reed shaken by the wind” bends whichever way the wind blows. John was not that kind of man. He spoke the truth even to a king, and he went to prison for it.
7.notes: Reeds grew along the Jordan River, where John baptized.

8.brief: Jesus asks whether they went to see a man in soft clothing, since such people live in kings’ palaces. John was no courtier seeking comfort, and his faithfulness has landed him in a king’s prison instead.
8.explain:
“But what did you go out to see? A man clothed in soft garments?”

Did they go out to see a man in fine clothes? John wore camel’s hair and a leather belt (3:4).

“Indeed, those who wear soft clothing are in kings’ houses.”

People who wear luxurious clothing live in palaces. John was in a king’s prison, not a king’s palace.
8.notes: The Greek word translated “soft” describes fine, luxurious cloth.

9.brief: Jesus asks whether they went out to see a prophet, and affirms that John is a prophet “and more than a prophet.” John holds a unique place among God’s messengers.
9.explain:
“But what did you go out to see? A prophet?”

Jesus asks a third time. Did they go out to see “a prophet”? Yes. The people regarded John as a prophet (21:26).

“Yes, I say to you, and more than a prophet.”

John was a prophet, but he was more than that. He was the one whom the prophets themselves foretold.
9.notes: The prophets spoke about the Messiah. John was the only one who pointed to Him in person.

10.brief: John is the one of whom Scripture says, “Behold, I send My messenger before Your face, Who will prepare Your way before You.” As Malachi foretold, John is the forerunner who prepares the way for the Lord’s coming in Jesus.
10.explain:
“For this is he of whom it is written:”

Jesus identifies John from Scripture.

“Behold, I send My messenger before Your face, Who will prepare Your way before You.”

The quotation draws on Malachi 3:1. God promised to send His “messenger” ahead of Him to prepare the way. John is that messenger. He prepared the way for Jesus.

In Malachi, the messenger prepares the way before the LORD Himself. By applying the words to John and Himself, Jesus identifies His own coming with the coming of the LORD.
10.notes: The wording also echoes Exodus 23:20, where God promises to send an Angel before Israel. The Greek word for messenger is also the word for angel.

11.brief: No one born of women has risen greater than John the Baptist, yet the least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he. John stands at the threshold of the kingdom, and the privilege of sharing in its arrival surpasses even his great role.
11.explain:
“Assuredly, I say to you, among those born of women there has not risen one greater than John the Baptist;”

Jesus gives John the highest praise. No one born of a woman, that is, no human being, has been greater than John. His role in God’s plan was unique.

“but he who is least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he.”

Yet the smallest person in God’s kingdom is greater than John. This is not a judgment on John’s character or salvation. John stood at the turning point between the age of promise and the arrival of the kingdom. The least person in the kingdom has a greater privilege. He lives in the time of fulfillment that John only announced.
11.notes: The Greek word translated “least” is the comparative form, literally lesser. It may mean the lesser one in the kingdom.

12.brief: From the days of John until now “the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent take it by force.” As John’s imprisonment shows, the kingdom and its messengers are meeting violent opposition from those who resist it.
12.explain:
“And from the days of John the Baptist until now the kingdom of heaven suffers violence,”

Since John began preaching, the kingdom has faced “violence.” John himself sits in prison. Jesus faces growing hostility. The kingdom and its messengers are under attack.

“and the violent take it by force.”

“The violent” are those who oppose the kingdom. They try to seize it and destroy it. Herod’s imprisonment of John is a clear example.
12.notes: The Greek verb in the first half has the same form whether it means the kingdom is being acted on or the kingdom is acting. Read the first way, as the NKJV does, the kingdom suffers violence. That fits John’s imprisonment and the hostility Jesus faces. Read the second way, the verb describes the kingdom advancing forcefully. Luke 16:16 uses the same verb form in a different saying, where people are pressing into the kingdom. That saying supports reading the response to the kingdom as eager entry rather than opposition. In Matthew’s setting, the NKJV reading of violent opposition remains primary.

13.brief: All the prophets and the law prophesied until John. John marks the end of the era of promise and the arrival of what the prophets foretold.
13.explain:
“For all the prophets and the law prophesied until John.”

The whole Old Testament looked forward to the coming of God’s kingdom. That time of prophecy reached its end with John. With Jesus, fulfillment has arrived.
13.notes: Matthew usually writes the Law and the Prophets (5:17; 7:12; 22:40). Here the order is reversed, perhaps to stress the prophetic character of the whole Scripture.

14.brief: If they are willing to accept it, John is the Elijah who was to come. John is not Elijah returned in person, but he fulfills Malachi’s promise by coming in Elijah’s spirit and power.
14.explain:
“And if you are willing to receive it,”

Jesus knows this teaching will be hard for some to accept.

“he is Elijah who is to come.”

Malachi 4:5 promised that God would send Elijah the prophet before the great day of the LORD. Jesus says John is that “Elijah.”

John himself denied being Elijah when he was asked (John 1:21). He was not Elijah returned in person. But he fulfilled Malachi’s prophecy by coming in the spirit and power of Elijah, as the angel told his father (Luke 1:17). Like Elijah, John called God’s people to turn back to Him.
14.notes: Jesus says the same in 17:10–13, and the disciples understand that He was speaking of John the Baptist.

15.brief: Jesus urges, “He who has ears to hear, let him hear!” Understanding who John is, and therefore who Jesus is, calls for attentive and willing hearing.
15.explain:
“He who has ears to hear, let him hear!”

Jesus calls His listeners to pay attention. Everyone can hear the words, but not everyone will understand and accept them. This saying calls for a response.
15.notes: Jesus uses the same saying after the parable of the sower (13:9) and the explanation of the wheat and tares (13:43).

16.brief: Jesus asks what this generation is like and compares it to children sitting in the marketplaces calling to their companions. He describes the attitude of the people who have rejected both John and Himself.
16.explain:
“But to what shall I liken this generation?”

Jesus compares the people of His time to something familiar.

“It is like children sitting in the marketplaces and calling to their companions,”

The picture is of children playing in the town square. One group calls to the other, wanting them to join a game.
16.notes: The phrase this generation refers to the people of Jesus’ day who heard John and Jesus but did not respond.

17.brief: The children complain, “We played the flute for you, And you did not dance; We mourned to you, And you did not lament.” Like sulky children, this generation refuses to respond to any call, whether joyful or sorrowful.
17.explain:
“and saying: ‘We played the flute for you, And you did not dance;”

Some children want to play a wedding game. They play happy music, but the others will not dance.

“We mourned to you, And you did not lament.”

Then they try a funeral game. They sing a sad song, but the others will not mourn. The other children refuse every game. Nothing satisfies them.
17.notes: Weddings were celebrated with flute music and dancing. Funerals included wailing and lament (9:23).

18.brief: John came neither eating nor drinking, and they said, “He has a demon.” They dismissed John’s austere call to repentance as madness.
18.explain:
“For John came neither eating nor drinking,”

John lived a life of self-denial. He fasted, ate locusts and wild honey, and drank no wine (Luke 1:15). His life was like the funeral song.

“and they say, ‘He has a demon.”

The people rejected John. They said he was demon-possessed. His austerity became their excuse.
18.notes: John’s message called for repentance and mourning over sin.

19.brief: The Son of Man came eating and drinking, and they called Him “a glutton and a winebibber, a friend of tax collectors and sinners!” but wisdom is shown right by her children. They rejected Jesus’ welcome to sinners just as they rejected John, yet the fruit of God’s wisdom in both ministries proves it true.
19.explain:
“The Son of Man came eating and drinking,”

Jesus came in the opposite way. He ate and drank with people and attended feasts. His life was like the wedding song.

“and they say, ‘Look, a glutton and a winebibber, a friend of tax collectors and sinners!”

The people rejected Jesus too. They called Him “a glutton and a winebibber,” someone who eats and drinks too much. They called Him “a friend of tax collectors and sinners.” That much was true, as Matthew’s own story shows (9:10–13). They meant it as an insult. It was really a description of His mercy.

“But wisdom is justified by her children.”

God’s “wisdom” is shown to be right by its results. The lives changed through John’s and Jesus’ ministries prove that God was at work in both.
19.notes:
Some manuscripts read by her works instead of by her children. Luke 7:35 reads by all her children.

Deuteronomy 21:20 describes a rebellious son as a glutton and a drunkard.

20.brief: Jesus begins to rebuke the cities where most of His mighty works were done, because they did not repent. These towns saw His power firsthand yet refused to turn to God.
20.explain:
“Then He began to rebuke the cities in which most of His mighty works had been done,”

Jesus now speaks against the towns where He had done most of His miracles. These towns had seen more of His power than any others.

“because they did not repent:”

The reason for His rebuke is clear. They did not repent. They were amazed, but they did not turn to God.
20.notes: The Greek word translated “mighty works” means acts of power.

21.brief: Jesus pronounces woe on Chorazin and Bethsaida, saying that if Tyre and Sidon had seen such works, they would have repented long ago in sackcloth and ashes. Gentile cities known for pride would have responded better than these privileged Jewish towns.
21.explain:
“Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida!”

“Woe” is a cry of grief and a warning of judgment. “Chorazin” was a town about two miles north of Capernaum. “Bethsaida” was on the northern shore of the Sea of Galilee. It was the hometown of Peter, Andrew, and Philip (John 1:44).

“For if the mighty works which were done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon,”

“Tyre and Sidon” were Gentile cities on the Mediterranean coast. The prophets condemned them for their pride and wickedness (Isaiah 23; Ezekiel 26–28).

“they would have repented long ago in sackcloth and ashes.”

Jesus says these pagan cities would have repented if they had seen what Chorazin and Bethsaida saw. “Sackcloth and ashes” were signs of grief and repentance.
21.notes: The Gospels record no miracles in Chorazin, and only one in Bethsaida (Mark 8:22–26). Jesus’ words show that He did many works there that are not recorded (John 21:25).

22.brief: Jesus tells Chorazin and Bethsaida that it will be more tolerable for Tyre and Sidon on the day of judgment than for them. Greater light brings greater accountability before God.
22.explain:
“But I say to you, it will be more tolerable for Tyre and Sidon in the day of judgment than for you.”

Judgment will be worse for the Galilean towns than for Tyre and Sidon. Greater light brings greater accountability. Those who saw more will answer for more.
22.notes: Jesus teaches the same principle in Luke 12:48: to whom much is given, from him much will be required.

23.brief: Jesus warns Capernaum, which was lifted up to heaven, that it will be brought down to Hades, for if Sodom had seen His works, it would still remain. Capernaum, Jesus’ own home base, has been exalted by His presence, yet its unbelief will bring it low.
23.explain:
“And you, Capernaum, who are exalted to heaven, will be brought down to Hades;”

Jesus turns to “Capernaum,” His own home base (4:13). Capernaum had been lifted up by Jesus’ presence. It saw more of His works than any other town. But it will be “brought down to Hades.”

His words echo Isaiah 14:13–15, where the king of Babylon says he will ascend into heaven but is brought down to Sheol.

“for if the mighty works which were done in you had been done in Sodom, it would have remained until this day.”

Even “Sodom,” the city destroyed for its wickedness (Genesis 19:24–25), would have repented if it had seen what Capernaum saw.
23.notes: The Greek word translated “Hades” refers to the realm of the dead. Here it pictures complete humiliation and judgment.

24.brief: Jesus tells Capernaum that it will be more tolerable for the land of Sodom on the day of judgment than for it. Having seen Jesus’ mighty works and refused Him, Capernaum will face a heavier judgment than Sodom, which saw no such works.
24.explain:
“But I say to you that it shall be more tolerable for the land of Sodom in the day of judgment than for you.”

Capernaum’s judgment will be worse than Sodom’s. Jesus had said the same of towns that reject His messengers (10:15). These warnings are real. They call everyone who hears the gospel to respond.
24.notes: Today the site of Capernaum lies in ruins, as do Chorazin and Bethsaida.

25.brief: Jesus thanks the Father, Lord of heaven and earth, for hiding these things from the wise and prudent and revealing them to babes. The Father reveals the truth about His Son not to the self-sufficient but to the humble and dependent.
25.explain:
“At that time Jesus answered and said,”

The tone changes from warning to prayer. In the middle of rejection, Jesus turns to His Father.

“I thank You, Father, Lord of heaven and earth,”

Jesus calls God “Father” and “Lord of heaven and earth.” He speaks with closeness and with reverence for God’s rule over all.

“that You have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and have revealed them to babes.”

Jesus thanks the Father for hiding the truth about the kingdom from “the wise and prudent” and revealing it to “babes.” The wise are people who trust their own learning, like the scribes and Pharisees. The babes are humble people, like the disciples, who receive God’s truth with simple trust.

God does not reject learning. He resists pride. The humble receive what the proud refuse.
25.notes: Paul makes a similar point in 1 Corinthians 1:26–29: God chose the foolish things of the world to put to shame the wise.

26.brief: Jesus affirms, “Even so, Father, for so it seemed good in Your sight.” He rests in the Father’s good and gracious will.
26.explain:
“Even so, Father, for so it seemed good in Your sight.”

Jesus rests in the Father’s will. This is how God has chosen to work, and it is good. Jesus does not question it.
26.notes: The Greek word translated “seemed good” describes God’s good pleasure. It appears in the Father’s words at Jesus’ baptism (3:17).

27.brief: All things have been handed over to Jesus by the Father, and no one truly knows the Son except the Father, nor the Father except the Son and those to whom the Son chooses to reveal Him. Jesus holds a unique relationship with the Father, and only through Him can anyone truly know God.
27.explain:
“All things have been delivered to Me by My Father,”

Jesus makes a great claim. The Father has given “all things” to Him. This includes all authority and all knowledge of God. Jesus will say after His resurrection that all authority in heaven and on earth has been given to Him (28:18).

“and no one knows the Son except the Father.”

The relationship between Father and Son is unique. Only the Father fully knows the Son.

“Nor does anyone know the Father except the Son, and the one to whom the Son wills to reveal Him.”

Only the Son fully knows the Father. No one can know God unless the Son reveals Him. Jesus is the only way to know the Father (John 14:6).
27.notes: John 1:18 says that no one has seen God at any time, but the only begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, has declared Him.

28.brief: Jesus invites, “Come to Me, all you who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.” He calls everyone weighed down by sin and the exhausting effort of self-reliance to come to Him and receive rest as a gift.
28.explain:
“Come to Me, all you who labor and are heavy laden,”

The One who alone reveals the Father now invites everyone to come to Him. The invitation is for “all.” It is for those who “labor,” who are worn out from effort, and for those who are “heavy laden,” weighed down by burdens.

People carry many burdens: sin, guilt, self-reliance, pride, comparison with others, and the need to prove themselves. Many in Jesus’ day were also burdened by the heavy demands the religious leaders placed on them (23:4).

“and I will give you rest.”

Jesus promises rest. This rest is His gift. It is given to everyone who comes to Him. It is the rest of forgiveness and peace with God, received by coming to Jesus.
28.notes: The Greek verb translated “give rest” means to refresh or relieve.

29.brief: Jesus says to take His yoke, learn from Him, because He is gentle and lowly in heart, and they will find rest for their souls. Coming to Jesus leads into a life under His rule and instruction, where disciples learn His meekness and humility and find a deeper rest within.
29.explain:
“Take My yoke upon you and learn from Me,”

A “yoke” was a wooden frame that joined animals together for work. Teachers spoke of taking on the yoke of the law. Jesus invites people to take His yoke, to come under His teaching and authority and to learn from Him.

“for I am gentle and lowly in heart,”

Jesus is not a harsh master. He is meek and humble. He does not crush those who come to Him.

“and you will find rest for your souls.”

There is a second rest here. In 11:28 Jesus gives rest to those who come to Him. Here, those who take His yoke and learn from Him “will find rest.” This rest is discovered as disciples live under His instruction and become gentle and humble like Him. Pride, self-reliance, and the need to prove ourselves give way to dependence on Him.
29.notes: The phrase rest for your souls comes from Jeremiah 6:16, where God tells His people to walk in the old paths: “Then you will find rest for your souls.”

30.brief: Jesus explains, “For My yoke is easy and My burden is light.” His rule is not crushing like the burdens of pride and self-effort, because He carries His people in relationship with Himself.
30.explain:
“For My yoke is easy and My burden is light.”

Jesus’ “yoke” still carries a “burden.” Following Him still involves obedience and work. But His yoke fits well. It is “easy” in the sense of kind and well-suited. His burden is “light.” He carries it with His disciples.

This does not promise an easy outward life. Jesus has just warned His disciples of persecution (10:16–39). It promises rest in relationship with Him, whatever comes.
30.notes:
The Greek word translated “easy” means kind, good, or well-fitting. It is used of God’s kindness in Luke 6:35.

1 John 5:3 says that God’s commandments are not burdensome.
